activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
story:
Grayson set the shoebox on the kitchen table and lifted out the photo of his grandfather in his straw hat, holding a fishing pole he never actually used. "It has to be right," he told his mom, who was peeling clementines and not looking at him. "He's only going to get one chance to find his way back."

Ariane arrived at four o'clock with her arms full. She had brought a stack of papel picado her aunt had mailed from Guanajuato, a fat bundle of marigolds from the flower shop, and her little brother Cohen, who wanted to help and kept trying to help too much. "We put it up on November first and second," Ariane said, sliding the paper banners across the table. "My family does it every year. Dia de los Muertos." She was usually quiet in class, the kind of person who let other kids talk over her, but today she was assertive about every detail, like a coach calling plays.

Grayson remembered the summer before last, when his grandfather sat on the porch steps shelling pistachios and telling him about a documentary he'd watched on the tundra, how the caribou knew exactly when to move even though nobody printed them a map. Grayson had asked how they knew, and his grandfather had shrugged and said, "Some things find their way without being told." Grayson had thought that was just something old people said. Now he wanted it to be true.

He built the altar on the sideboard, two wooden crates stacked and draped with a cloth. Cohen handed him the photo and Grayson set it at the center, where his grandfather could look out at the whole room. Then he pulled off marigold petals and scattered them in a line from the front door to the altar, orange against the floorboards like a lit fuse running backward. "The color and the scent guide spirits home," Ariane said, adjusting a candle Cohen had knocked crooked. "That's the whole idea." She wanted this to work too, Grayson realized. Her own grandmother's photo was on an altar in her house right now, and she had looked at it before walking over.

Cohen kept rearranging the food offerings, moving the pan dulce to the left, then back to the right, testing where it belonged. Grayson started to contradict him, then stopped. "Put it where you think he'd find it first," he said. Cohen placed the sweet bread directly in front of the photo, dead center, and stepped back with his hands on his hips like he had solved something.

They sat together as the sky outside went from orange to blue to black. Nobody talked much. Grayson leaned close to the marigolds and breathed in, sharp and dusty-sweet, memorizing it the way you'd memorize a password. If his grandfather was going to follow that smell through the dark, then Grayson wanted to know it himself, in case he ever had to call it back to mind.

The candle flickered once, and Cohen whispered, "He's reading the menu."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
The drama room smelled like dust and old curtains, and Mr. Wu had pushed the desks against the wall to make an empty space in the middle. Leo stood at the edge of it with his hands in his pockets. In two weeks the class would perform short improvised scenes for the whole seventh grade, and Leo wanted a good one, but yesterday his scene with Kashton had collapsed in thirty seconds. They had argued about whether they were astronauts or chefs, and the audience had laughed at them, not with them.

"Partners again," Mr. Wu said, reading from his clipboard. "Leo and Pearl."

Pearl walked to the center, rolled her shoulders, and started the scene before Leo was ready. She pinched an invisible cord, made a casting motion, and reeled slowly. "Big one out there today, Grandpa," she said. "Bigger than the one that got away last summer."

Leo heard the words but not the rest. He stared at her empty hands and said, "What are you doing? We're not fishing, we're at a bank."

Pearl's arms dropped. The scene went quiet, and someone in the back snickered. Mr. Wu tapped his clipboard twice, and the class paused.

Leo frowned at Pearl. "You didn't say we were fishing. You just wiggled your arm."

"She did say it," said Kashton from the side. "With the rod. Mr. Wu told us yesterday, remember? An offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, like a place, a name, or a problem. The rod was the place. The lake."

Leo turned it over in his head. Offers could be invisible things, not just words. That was the hidden part, like figuring out which key opened a stuck lock. He thought of a way to test it. He would ignore nothing and see how long the scene could run.

"Same scene," Mr. Wu said. "From the top, and this time, accept it. Yes, and."

Pearl cast the invisible line again. "Big one today, Grandpa."

"Yes, and it's going to demolish the dock if we drag it in," Leo said, grabbing the rod with both hands. "Remember when your antibiotic pills spilled in the tackle box and the whole boat smelled like a pharmacy?"

"Fish loved it," Pearl said. "That patch of water was fertile. Best catches of my life."

They hauled and staggered, and Kashton called out from the side, "The dock is breaking!" so Leo tipped sideways, pulling Pearl with him, and the class clapped while the two of them sprawled on the floor, still holding the rod that wasn't there.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors, because an odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one.
story:
Alexa slid her laptop toward the middle of the table in the library corner where coding club met every Thursday. Mr. Novák had given them one hour before the mini-showcase at four thirty, when each of them would stand up and run a program for the rest of the club. Her objective was small but stubborn: a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. Her first version worked, but when she typed a big number like 999,983, the little spinner just sat there, thinking, while the clock on the wall ticked closer to the deadline.

Tessa leaned over from the next seat. "Mine keeps saying 9 is prime. Can I look at yours?"

"Watch this, though," Alexa said. She typed 999,983 again and they both stared at the cursor blinking in the terminal, doing nothing. "It's testing every single number up to it. Even ones that can't possibly work."

She wrote the numbers out on scrap paper to think it through. Her loop tried 2, then 3, then 4, then 5, then 6. She circled the even ones after 2 and frowned at them. A number like 999,983 was odd, and every second thing her loop tested was even. She tested a smaller case to be sure, checking whether 15 could divide evenly by 4 or by 6. It couldn't, not once, not ever. After checking whether a number was divisible by 2, a program only needed to test odd divisors, because an odd number could never be divided evenly by an even one. She sat back. Half the loop was pure waste.

While she typed the fix, starting her divisors at 3 and stepping by 2 instead of 1, Mika appeared behind her chair, holding a folded note he had passed across the room like they were in regular class. Alexa unfolded it. "Trade you my variable-naming tips for a look at your loop trick," it read, with a small doodle of a turtle. "My checker takes forever on anything past 1000." She wrote "deal, after showcase" on the bottom, folded it back, and handed it over her shoulder without turning around.

At 4:28 she pressed Enter on 999,983. The answer, "prime," appeared before the second hand finished its trip around the clock face. Mr. Novák called two minutes, and Tessa closed her laptop, still grinning about her own bug, which had turned out to be a missing equals sign hiding in the plumbing of her if-statement. When it was Alexa's turn, she stood, typed one last number into the prompt, and said, "Watch how fast it comes back."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount deposited, called the principal, so it adds the same dollar amount every year.
story:
Victoria spread her bank statements across the library table like a detective who had just found a suspicious fingerprint. Five statements, five years, one question that had been bugging her since math class.

"Kylian, look at this. Every single year, the interest is exactly twelve dollars. Not eleven fifty. Not twelve twenty. Twelve."

Kylian leaned over, chewing the end of his pencil. He wanted the library's chess set for lunch period, and Ms. Ndlovu had told him he could have it if he finished his math work first, which was why he was stuck at this table instead of planning his opening moves. "Maybe your bank is just lazy."

"That's what I thought at first." Victoria tapped the page. "But Ms. Ndlovu said there's a rule that governs this, and rules aren't lazy. Rules are rules." She remembered, suddenly, the day her grandfather had opened the account for her. She'd been seven, and he'd slid the paper across the bank counter and said, "Watch this money grow, kiddo," and she'd imagined an actual plant sprouting dollar bills. It had not sprouted. It had just sat there, adding twelve dollars a year like clockwork.

"Okay," she said, sitting up straight. "Test time. If the interest only ever counts my original hundred dollars, then it adds the same amount every year. Watch. Year one, twelve. Year two, twelve. All the way down. It fits." She flipped to a different sheet, one she'd made up herself, with numbers that grew every year instead of staying the same. "But if interest counted the whole balance, the interest itself would grow too. Kylian, my bank is only paying me on the original amount."

"The original amount," Kylian said slowly, "is called the principal. Ms. Ndlovu drilled that into us Tuesday. You were drawing on your shoe."

"I was taking notes artistically." Victoria pulled her shoe closer and, sure enough, there was the word, inked in blue along the heel. She laughed so hard a boy at the next table shushed her with great compassion, as though she were a wounded bird rather than a girl cackling at her own sneakers.

"So compound interest is the one where you earn interest on your interest," Kylian said. "Simple is just principal, principal, principal."

"And my account is the boring one." Victoria sighed. Then she frowned. "Wait. Tuesday, you said the class voted on which bank to use for the fake class savings project."

"Yeah. Mackenzie's group won. They picked compound."

Victoria grabbed her notebook. Mackenzie's group had gotten five extra fake dollars over five years on the very same starting amount. Extra money, from nothing but a different rule. She looked at her own statements, all those identical twelves marching in a row, and felt the future shift under her like a rug being pulled.

"Grandpa's getting a phone call tonight," she said, and began stuffing the statements into her backpack. "Right after I beat you at chess."

"You can't have the chess set. I earned it."

"Then watch me earn something better."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
story:
Emilie held the onion like it was a live grenade, which, considering her last attempt, was fair. "Curve your fingers under, like a claw," said Ms. Hu, the camp cook who had already confiscated one bandage box. Emilie bent her fingertips until her knuckles led the way, set the knife against them, and chopped straight down. The pieces were uneven, but all ten fingers stayed where they belonged, so she counted it as a win. Miller gave her a slow clap from across the picnic table.

The real prize, though, was the sauce. Emilie's group had been assigned pasta with sauce from scratch, and she was determined not to serve what Quinn's group served last summer, which everyone still called red water. She diced tomatoes, crushed garlic, dumped it all in the pot with a splash of oil, and set it over the fire with the lid on, because a lid kept things from burning, obviously.

Twenty minutes later she lifted the lid and stared. The sauce was thin. Really thin. Quinn leaned over and said, "Congratulations, you've invented soup." Emilie stirred it and thought about it. When you boil water for tea, the steam fogs up the window, and the pan ends up emptier than it started. Water leaves as steam. Steam can't leave if the lid is on. She did a quick analysis of her own logic: lid on, steam trapped, water stays, sauce runny. Lid off, water escapes, sauce thickens. It was a theory, and theories could be tested.

She propped the lid on a rock beside the fire and let the pot sit uncovered, bubbling slowly. Miller watched the steam curl up into the pines. "It smells more like sauce already," he admitted, which was generous, since it had always smelled like sauce. Emilie stirred every few minutes and marked the sauce line on the wooden spoon with her thumbnail so she could track it.

By dinnertime the spoon told the truth. The sauce had crept down past her thumbnail, thicker, clingier, sticking to the pasta instead of pooling under it. Even the second-in-command taste tester, a kid who usually ate hot dogs and nothing else, asked for seconds. Ms. Hu raised an eyebrow at the empty lid, sitting barren on its rock, and said nothing at all.

"That's my analysis," Emilie announced, ladling out the last of it. "Steam out, sauce thick." Quinn held up his fork. "Less analysis, more pasta."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
story:
Ivy's mother had banned screens for the weekend, so naturally Ivy spent Saturday at her mother's office, learning to use one. It was a kind of quiet rebellion: her mother had said "no games," and Ivy had decided that a spreadsheet was clearly not a game.

The task was real. Her mother's team had sold raffle tickets all week, and someone had to add up the columns for each seller and turn them into a bar chart for Monday's meeting. Her mother showed her once, typed "=SUM(B2:B8)" into a cell, and got pulled away to a phone call. Ivy tried it in the next column and got a number that made no sense at all. Liyana, whose mother worked two desks over, leaned in and studied the screen. "Layla's going to accuse you of cheating," she said. "Her chart's going to show her losing to a wrong number."

Ivy stared at the formula. It looked exactly like her mother's. She clicked through the cells one at a time, reading them aloud, and found the problem near the bottom: row 12 sat outside the range, holding sixty-two tickets all by itself. The formula was obeying her perfectly. It was just doing what she'd told it to do instead of what she'd meant. She changed it to "=SUM(B2:B12)," and the total jumped.

"That's the thing about these programs," said a voice behind her. It was her grandmother, who still came in on Saturdays to sort the mail. "They do the arithmetic so you can't argue with it. The first one for home computers was called VisiCalc. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it came out in 1979 for the Apple II." She peered at the screen. "Before that, I did budgets on paper, and every total was a small act of hope."

Ivy tested the fix before trusting it. She picked the column with the fewest numbers, added them in her head, and compared. It matched. Then she highlighted the totals, clicked the bar chart button, and watched the bars rise like a skyline, Layla's towering over everyone's except one mystery bar. "Whose is that?" Liyana asked.

They traced the column header up. It was labeled GRANDMA.

Her grandmother raised her hands. "I sold to the whole mailroom."

"You didn't tell me you were in the raffle," Ivy said.

"You never asked."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
story:
Luke set his phone face down beside his plate and poked at his noodles. "Dad, I need to say something about the thing you sent me this morning."

His dad looked up. The link had been a blog post claiming that a certain tea could shrink your risk of getting sick by half. Luke had wanted to believe it, because his grandmother drank that tea every day and still caught every cold that went through her building. Something about that didn't fit, and it had bugged him all through school.

"Ocean and I looked it up at lunch," Luke said. "We found the blog post, but then we found a real article in a science journal about the same tea, and the journal one said the effect was tiny, like barely anything." He picked up his fork and held it perpendicular to the table, twirling noodles around it while he talked. "So I asked Ms. Szabó after school what the difference was. She didn't tell me the answer. She just pulled up both articles side by side and said one question would sort it out: who checked each one before it went out."

His little sister reached across for the salt, knocking over the pepper shaker, and their mom set it upright without looking up from her plate.

"The blog post? Nobody checked it," Luke said. "The guy just wrote it and clicked publish. But the journal article, before it got printed, other experts in the field reviewed it for errors. Ms. Szabó said it's called peer review. So one is a story about one person's opinion, and the other is a claim that a bunch of scientists already tried to poke holes in and couldn't. Well, mostly couldn't. The journal one even lists what's still uncertain."

Dad leaned back. "So you're telling me my tea thing is wrong."

"I'm telling you it's untested," Luke said. "There's a difference." His dad laughed, but Luke noticed he slid his own phone over and opened the link again, scrolling slower this time. Luke felt his shoulders, which had been bunched up like a fist, finally start to unclench.

"Grandma should keep drinking it if she likes it," Mom said. "Tastes good, keeps her company. Just don't buy the thirty-dollar kind."

"Deal," Dad said. Then he turned the screen toward Luke. "Okay, expert. Show me how you found the journal one."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
story:
Mathis had one goal at the library: finish his current events assignment before Saturday, when the skate park opened and his whole weekend disappeared. The assignment asked for a letter to the editor, which sounded easy until he read the example his teacher had circled in the local paper. "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." He copied it onto his notepad and then sat there chewing his pencil, because something about it itched.

Bronson dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of car magazines he had no intention of reading. "That letter about the park? My dad read it out at dinner and laughed. Then he and my uncle argued for an hour." Bronson leaned in, lowering his voice the way he did when he wanted to confide something. "I think my uncle wants the letter writer to be right. He hates the park. He says two million dollars could have fixed the pool."

That word, two million, was the itch. Mathis marched to the reference desk, where Mr. Szabó was repairing a spine with tissue paper and a tiny brush, and asked where he could find out what the park actually cost. Mr. Szabó pointed him to the municipal records on microfilm, then to the town website, and within ten minutes Mathis had a budget document on the screen. Two million dollars. He wrote the number down twice to be sure. The letter writer hadn't invented it. A small fracture appeared in his plan to write a letter calling the whole thing nonsense.

Lauralie appeared beside him with her own assignment sheet, peering at his screen. "So the guy's right?"

"The number's right," Mathis said slowly. "The rest is..." He read the sentence again. "The cost part, I can check. I just did. But 'a waste' isn't a number. Nobody can look that up. That's just him."

"Then my uncle was arguing about the wrong thing at dinner," Bronson said, sounding almost betrayed.

"There was a significant amount of mashed potato involved, apparently," Lauralie said, and Mr. Szabó, without looking up from his brush, made a small noise that might have been a laugh.

Mathis wrote his own letter right there at the table. He stated the cost, which he had verified, and then wrote that in his opinion the park was worth it, and that anyone who disagreed should come watch on Saturday. Lauralie read it over his shoulder and said the last sentence sounded like a dare. He kept it anyway.

He slid the finished page into his backpack, and Bronson raised his hand as if taking an oath. "If your uncle shows up at the park," Mathis said, "tell him to bring the letter."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: In the dark, the eyes slowly grow more sensitive as rod cells in the retina rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, which takes half an hour or more.
story:
The lights went out just as Bennett was carrying a bowl of noodles across the kitchen, and in the sudden blackness he walked the bowl straight into the counter. Noodles everywhere. His little sister wailed from the living room, and his mother's voice came out of the dark, calm but tired, asking if anyone knew where the flashlight had gone. Nobody did. Bennett felt along the wall to the junk drawer and found batteries, rubber bands, a takeout menu, and no flashlight.

"Check your phone," his mother said. He did. Nine percent. He budgeted that carefully, using it only in quick flashes, because the power company's recording said the outage covered their whole street and might last the evening. There was a battery lantern in the shed at the back of the yard, left over from their camping trip, if he could find the shed, and the lantern, and the latch that always stuck. On his first attempt he made it three steps off the porch and nearly tripped over the rake he knew he had left somewhere out there. The yard was a single black wall. He held his hand an inch from his face and could barely make out its shape.

He called Jordan, whose house still had power on the other side of town. "Your eyes get better in the dark," Jordan said. "My sister's science book is right here. It says rod cells in your retina rebuild something called rhodopsin, and that takes half an hour or more." Bennett said that felt like forever. Jordan said that's what the book said, and then his mother called him for dinner and he was gone.

Half an hour felt longer than it sounded. Bennett's sister was scared of the dark hallway, so he sat with her on the couch and they played a guessing game where one of them made a sound with something from the kitchen drawer and the other named it. Spoon, whisk, the weird thing that might be a garlic press. He made her laugh with the whisk. His mother found candles in the bathroom cabinet but saved them, saying she'd rather keep them in case the night got longer.

After what he guessed was about half an hour, Bennett noticed he could see the couch cushions as separate shapes, then the doorway, then the rake lying in the grass, its handle a pale line in the moonlight. His eyes had turned into something useful. He hadn't done anything except wait, but it felt like a small victory, and he wanted to use it before it was wasted. "Stay on the porch," he told his sister. "I'm getting the lantern." He counted his steps to the shed, twelve, and his hand found the stubborn latch on the first try.

Inside the shed the lantern was exactly where he remembered, on the shelf above the bikes, and when he thumbed the switch it blazed to life. The whole yard jumped out of the blackness, the fence, the swing set, his sister on the porch steps with her hands over her eyes, peeking through her fingers. "Don't point it at people," he said, tilting it toward the grass. "It'll wreck your night eyes." He had figured that out himself, after the lantern's beam left a purple blot floating in his vision for a full minute.

Mr. Eze from next door called over the fence that his power was out too, and Bennett carried the lantern to the gap in the hedge so the old man could see to reset something in his garage. When Bennett came back, his mother had set out bread and peanut butter on the kitchen counter. "Wash first," she said. "The dark is not an excuse to skip hygiene." He washed his hands by feel, dried them on the towel that hung where towels always hung, and made his sister a sandwich with the lantern propped on the counter behind them, aimed at the ceiling.

They ate on the porch steps in the deep blue dark, and Bennett noticed he could see pretty well now even where the lantern's light didn't reach, the vague shape of the swing set swaying a little in the wind. His sister leaned against his arm, half asleep, still holding her sandwich. Somewhere down the street a porch light popped on, and another, and then theirs blinked to life above the door.

"Turn it off," his sister whispered. "I want to keep my rhodopsin."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override can be renewed.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and paper, and the polling station behind the orange plastic barriers hummed with quiet voices. Ms. Lim had brought the whole class because their assignment was due by four o'clock: each of them had to read one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it, in their own words, to an adult who was actually voting today. Olivier had his photocopy of Section 2 folded into quarters in his jacket pocket, and he had read it so many times the creases were going soft.

"Which one did you get?" Jonah asked, bouncing on his heels near the information desk where a woman was flipping through a binder of voter names, some kind of database with everyone's address in it.

"Freedom of expression," Olivier said. Then, lower, "But I don't know if it's real."

Lyla stopped chewing her gum. "What do you mean, real?"

Olivier glanced toward the voting screens. Last Sunday at his grandfather's house, the news had been on, and his grandfather and his mother had argued right through dinner about something called the notwithstanding clause. His mother said it made rights useless. His grandfather said it kept judges from running the whole country. Olivier had sat in the hallway with his plate on his knees, listening, and one number had stuck in his head like a burr: five years.

He didn't tell them that yet. Instead he said, "Watch this," and walked over to the woman at the desk. "Excuse me. Do the rights in the Charter always apply?"

She looked up. "Always? Well." She tapped the binder. "There's a clause, I believe, where Parliament or a province can override some of them. My husband could recite the section number, I can't."

"But they come back?" Olivier pressed. "After how long?"

"That I do know, because of all the fuss on the news. Five years. Then it has to be renewed or it lapses." She turned back to her binder, and the line behind her shifted impatiently.

Olivier walked back to Jonah and Lyla with his heart going strangely fast. "Five years," he said. "The override lasts five years. And they can renew it." He let that sit. "So it's not that expression isn't a right. It is. It's that a government can set certain rights aside for five years at a time, and then do it again. My mom thinks that means they could just keep renewing forever, and freedom of expression would cease to mean anything."

"So is your right real or not?" Lyla asked.

Olivier thought of his grandfather's voice, stubborn, and his mother's, cold and certain. He unfolded his crumpled page. "It's real," he said slowly. "It's just not armor. It's more like a promise that can be broken by a specific rule, and the rule has a name and a clock on it." He looked up. "That's what I'll say. In my own words."

At four o'clock he stood beside the orange barrier with his page in his hand, and an older man with a folded ballot came out from behind the screen. Olivier stepped forward. "Can I tell you about Section 2?"

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: In the United States, falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged 65 and older.
story:
Chloe stood in the middle of the guest bedroom with a notebook and a mission. Grandma Ruth was arriving on Saturday to stay for a whole week, and Chloe had overheard her mom on the phone saying Grandma had seemed shaky lately. Chloe wanted this visit to be perfect, which meant the room had to be perfect too.

Her plan started because of something she'd read in the library while killing time before volleyball practice: in the United States, falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged 65 and older. She'd been skeptical at first. Falls? Not heart trouble or car accidents? But the fact had stuck in her head like a burr, and now she couldn't stop seeing hazards everywhere she looked. The loose braided rug by the bed. The lamp cord crossing the walking path to the door. The nightstand with its sharp corner, positioned exactly where a person stumbling in the dark would land.

She dragged the rug out into the hallway and taped the cord along the baseboard. Then she borrowed a night-light from the bathroom and plugged it in low, where its glow refracted off the mirror and sent a soft stripe across the floorboards. She wrote "test at night" in her notebook.

Addilyn came over Thursday to help, and she was skeptical about the whole project. "Your grandma has lived in houses for like seventy years," she said, sitting on the guest bed. "I don't think she needs a bodyguard." But Addilyn wanted to feel useful, so she claimed the job of checking the bathroom, and she turned out to be ruthless about it. She confiscated the bath mat, announced that its rubber backing had cracked, and taped a sticky note to the tub that said HOLD THE BAR.

That night Chloe ran her test. She turned off every light, waited five minutes in the dark hallway, then walked to the guest bed the way Grandma would, slow and half-asleep. Her shin found the nightstand corner on the first try, and she sat down hard on the carpet, biting her lip against the sting. The small flash of humiliation was worth it, though, because now she knew the corner was a real problem, not just a theory. She moved the nightstand to the window wall and put a chair in its place, one with rounded legs and nothing to trip over.

On Saturday, Grandma Ruth arrived with one suitcase and a tin of lemon cookies. When Chloe showed her the room, Grandma stood in the doorway for a long moment. "There's no rug," she said.

"I moved it," Chloe said. "Falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults sixty-five and older, in the United States. So I tested the room in the dark and everything."

Grandma set down the suitcase. Then she held out her arm. "Walk me in, then," she said. "And afterward, we investigate that tin of cookies."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Older adults are at greater risk of hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature, than younger adults.
story:
Noemie's grandfather had been at her house since Monday, and by Wednesday she had noticed something odd. Every evening he sat on the back step with his cardigan buttoned to the chin while the rest of the family was still in T-shirts, and when her mom asked if he was cold, he always said, "I'm fine, a bit of air does you good." Noemie had tried to conceal her worry behind a smile, but she kept count anyway: three evenings, three cardigans, three "I'm fine"s. Something did not add up, because grandfathers who are fine do not sit with their hands tucked under their arms like that.

On Thursday the whole plan for Saturday hung over everything: the family picnic at Riverside Park, which her grandfather had been looking forward to since before he arrived. The forecast said sunny but cold, only ten degrees by late afternoon when the games would happen. Noemie decided she could not just hope for the best. She needed evidence.

At school she found Charlize and Mariana on the bleachers and told them the whole thing, counting on her fingers. "He never complains," Noemie said. "That's the part that scares me. If he were complaining, I'd know what to do."

"Complaining is kind of subjective anyway," Charlize said, unwrapping a granola bar. "My brother complains when his socks are the wrong colour." Mariana snorted so hard she almost fell off the bench.

Mariana pulled out her phone. "My mom looks this stuff up for her job. Try the health site." Noemie typed carefully, scrolling past ads, until she found the page and read the key line out loud. "Older adults are at greater risk of hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature, than younger adults." She read it twice, then sat very still. "So he might actually be getting colder than he lets on, and his body might not handle it the way mine does."

"It says you should keep older people in warm rooms and warm clothes," Charlize said, reading over her shoulder. "That's not an opinion. That's a rule with a name."

Noemie had a theory, and like any scientist, or like the narrator of a mystery who insists on proof, she wanted to test it. On Friday evening she carried two mugs of tea out to the back step and sat beside her grandfather without saying anything about coats or cold. She wrapped her own hands around the hot mug and waited. Within four minutes, his hand crept over and held the mug too, and when she offered to swap, giving him the hotter one, he took it without a single word of protest. His "I'm fine" suddenly looked like a shield he used to conceal the truth, even from people who loved him. She warmed her hands on the evidence.

So on Saturday at Riverside Park, Noemie acted before anyone asked her to. She claimed the picnic table nearest the sunlit hillside, not the one in the shade by the Frisbee field that her grandfather had picked out. She spread the blanket herself, angled the food so he'd have to sit in the sunniest spot to reach the sandwiches, and when the wind picked up she produced a thermos of tea and a fleece blanket as casually as if she'd forgotten she was carrying them. Her grandfather looked at the blanket, then at her, and a slow grin crossed his face. "You're a sneaky one," he said, pulling it over his knees. "Sneaky, but I'll allow it." He ate two sandwiches, laughed hardest at her terrible Frisbee throws, and by the time the sky turned orange he was still warm to the touch when Noemie patted his shoulder on the walk back to the car.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate.
story:
Norah spread her history project across her grandmother's kitchen table: notes, a pencil, and a photocopy of a settler's diary from 1848 that Ms. Diallo had given the class. The assignment was to use the diary to explain why people moved west, and everyone else had already written a paragraph saying "for free land and a fresh start." Norah wanted something better, but the diary's cramped handwriting kept sliding away from her.

She remembered the day Ms. Diallo handed it out. In the flashback, Marwan had waved his copy and said, "Easy, just copy what the guy wrote." Jada had frowned and said the writing looked like chicken scratches, and Ms. Diallo had said only, "Question what you read." Norah had rolled her eyes then. Now, alone in the quiet kitchen, she finally understood what her teacher meant.

The diary said the settler's family crossed a river on "the tenth of April, when the floods were so aggressive that we nearly lost the oxen." Norah's grandmother kept a box of old papers in the parlor, including facsimiles of an 1848 territorial newspaper she used for her volunteer work at the historical society. Norah dug out the April issue and found the river report. The paper said the flood had peaked in late March and the river was low and calm by the second week of April. One of them was wrong, but which?

She tested a simple idea. If the flood ended in March, maybe the diary writer mixed up his months, or maybe the newspaper had gotten it wrong. In the box she also found a letter from the same settlement, dated April 14, 1848, complaining about dry roads and dust. Then she checked the government land records her grandmother kept copies of, which noted the family's claim that spring. The letter and the newspaper and the records all agreed, so the diary was the odd one out. "So that's how it works," Norah said out loud. "You check a diary against other sources, like letters, newspapers and government records, to see if its details are accurate."

Her grandmother came in with two mugs of cocoa and read Norah's notes over her shoulder. "You know the diary's still valuable," she said. "Even a mistake tells you something. Maybe the flood frightened him so badly the date got tangled with his fear."

Norah looked at the diary page again, at the shaky letters around the word "aggressive." Her new paragraph would explain the westward pull of cheap land, but it would also explain how she knew, and how one frightened settler had gotten his dates wrong. She picked up her pencil and wrote her first real sentence of the night: "The diary says April, but the evidence says March, and the evidence wins."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong; it is often written as "If... then..."
story:
Louis pushed the cart down aisle four of Hartley's Hardware, past bins of screws he had no reason to categorize by size, and stopped in front of the plumbing section. In his head, the plan was perfect: a long plastic trough, tilted, with dirt on one end and water poured from the other. His science fair model was going to show an estuary, the place where a river meets the sea, and he wanted to prove something about the muddy banks there. He just couldn't say what, yet.

"There you are," said Clemence, catching up with him. She held two spray bottles and a bag of grass seed. "So what's your hypothesis?"

Louis pulled his notebook from his back pocket. "Plants stop erosion," he read off the page.

Clemence frowned at it. "How would anyone prove that wrong, though? You can't test the whole world. What if you just said, plants keep a slope stable?"

"It's still too big," Louis said slowly. He turned the notebook over, then back. "It has to be a prediction. If something, then something." He chewed the end of his pencil. "If I plant grass on one slope and leave the other one bare, then the planted side loses less dirt when I pour water over both."

"Now that's testable," Clemence said, and he wrote it down, underlining it twice.

They were reaching for a bag of topsoil when Ms. Fischer, his neighbor from three doors down, appeared at the end of the aisle with a paintbrush in her hand. She raised her eyebrows at the cart. "Flood in your bedroom, Louis?"

"Science fair," he said. "Model estuary. One planted bank, one bare."

"Sounds like you'll want the caulk too," she said, pointing at a shelf behind him, and walked off toward the paint counter.

Louis stared after her. Why caulk? Then he remembered last year's disaster, the volcano that had leaked through the bottom seam all over the gym floor. He grabbed a tube.

The trouble came three days later, in his garage, with the fair only two nights away. The first trial was fine. The second trial was fine. On the third trial, the bare slope lost almost no dirt at all, and Louis stood frozen, watering can dripping, staring at the water pooling in the wrong corner.

"Clemence," he called. "The bare side. Look at it. It's barely washing anything down."

She crouched beside the trough. "Why would it change? Same dirt, same water." She ran a finger along the bottom edge and held it up, wet and glinting. "It's not draining. There's a gap under the divider, and half the water is sneaking under the dirt instead of over it."

Louis knelt down and looked. She was right. The caulk tube was still in the toolbox, unopened. He'd sealed the outer seams and missed the one inside, hidden under the soil where nobody could see it.

"Every trial since I moved the divider," he said, checking his notes, "the numbers went weird. That was it the whole time."

They pried the divider up, ran a fat bead of caulk along the hidden edge, and waited, saying nothing, while it cured. Then Louis refilled both slopes, planted side on the left, bare side on the right, and lifted the watering can.

"Trial four," he said. "Watch the bare one."

He poured, and the muddy water came down the bare slope in a rushing brown streak.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Glasses for astigmatism use cylindrical lenses, which bend light more in one direction than in the other.
story:
Mathis had known something was wrong for months, but he had blamed everything except his own eyes. He blamed the whiteboard at school for being too shiny, and the street signs for being printed too small, and once he blamed Ms. Byrne for writing "in a secret font." Then his mother booked him an eye appointment, and now a slim black case sat on his desk at home, holding his first pair of glasses.

He had wanted this moment for weeks, in a quiet, embarrassing way. Anna-Eve and Lyana both wore glasses, and they made it look easy, like a club he hadn't been recruited into yet. He opened the case, slid the glasses on, and the world snapped into focus so sharply that he laughed out loud. The grain of his desk, the individual needles on the tree outside his window, everything was crisp.

Then he tilted his head sideways, and the whole room stretched. The window became tall and narrow, like taffy being pulled. He sat up fast and tried it again, slower. Glasses on, head upright: normal. Glasses on, head tilted: stretched. He pulled them off, turned them ninety degrees in his hands, and held one lens up to his eye like a magnifying glass. Through the lens, held the usual way, the door looked like a door. When he rotated the lens, the door's edges slid and swelled, wider one way, thinner the other.

So it wasn't his head doing it, and it wasn't magic. It was the lens itself, and the direction it faced. He grabbed his notebook and wrote, "Lens bends light more in one direction than the other. Direction matters." His lenses were cylinders, he remembered the optometrist saying the word "astigmatism," and clearly cylindrical lenses worked like that, stretching things depending how they sat. Turning the glasses was the only variable he was changing, so the lens had to be the cause.

He texted Lyana, because she'd had glasses since third grade.

"Test for me. Turn your glasses sideways and tell me what you see."

She replied a minute later: "My floor is tilting and my cat looks stretched. Why am I doing this?"

"Because mine do it too. Cylindrical lenses bend light more one way than the other. It's the lens, not us."

"Anna-Eve says hers just get blurry. Hers are for nearsightedness, different kind."

Mathis looked at his notebook, then at the door, and rotated the lens one slow quarter turn. The doorknob stretched toward him like it wanted to shake hands.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: If a quoted line is a question, the question mark goes inside the quotation marks and the tag after it starts with a lowercase letter, as in "Where are you?" he asked.
story:
Muhammad slid his draft across the table so Marek could see it. "It's the scene where the guard catches the thief," he said. "Read the dialogue part."

Marek read aloud. ""Where did you hide the key?" He asked." He stopped and squinted at the page. "Why did you put a capital H on 'He asked'? It's not a new sentence, is it?"

Muhammad looked at the line. He hadn't really thought about it; he had just capitalized because it looked right on its own line. "I don't know," he admitted. He remembered, suddenly, last year's club, when he had handed in a story full of vague stage directions like "they talked for a while" because writing actual dialogue felt too hard. He had avoided the problem instead of solving it, and he still felt a little embarrassed about that. Maybe this time he could figure it out.

He pulled out a library book from his backpack, one with lots of conversation in it, and flipped until he found a question in quotation marks. "Look," he said, tapping the page. ""Are you coming with us?" she asked. Question mark inside the quotation marks, and then lowercase s on 'she asked.'" He flipped further and found another one, then another. Every time, the same pattern. It was like there was a hidden rule you couldn't see until you lined up enough examples.

Denise leaned over from the next table. "Are you two doing detective work without me?"

"Sort of," Muhammad said. He copied the pattern onto a sticky note: "Where are you?" he asked. Then he tested it against his own draft. The rule fit his sentence too. "So the question mark belongs inside the quotation marks," he said, "and the tag after it starts with lowercase."

"Show me," Denise said, so he did, and she copied it into her notebook like it was testimony from a witness she trusted completely.

Ms. Huang rang the little bell that meant sharing time. "Does anyone have a scene with a clear climax?" she asked.

Muhammad raised his hand, then hesitated. Last month he would have stayed quiet and let Denise go first. He stood up. "Mine's about a guard and a thief. The climax is where the guard asks the one question the thief can't dodge." He read the whole scene out loud, and when he reached the fixed line, ""Where did you hide the key?" he asked," he heard how smooth it sounded, no bump in the rhythm at all.

"That question lands hard," Ms. Huang said. "The whole scene turns on it."

Marek grinned and mimicked the guard's stern voice. ""Where did you hide the key?""

Denise laughed. "Do it again."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Logan sat cross-legged on Carter's bedroom floor with Carter's phone balanced on his knee, waiting for a page to load. He had one goal: find the old class blog from sixth grade, the one where everyone had posted their prediction essays about the future. Carter had bet him five dollars it was gone forever, deleted when the school switched websites.

"It'll say page not found," Carter said, chewing a granola bar over Logan's shoulder. "Dead links don't come back."

"Maybe not," Logan said. "But dead links leave ghosts." He wasn't sure what he meant until he said it, and then he liked it.

He typed the old address anyway, and sure enough the screen went grey with an error. Logan stared at the dead link and wondered where pages went when nobody hosted them anymore. Something had to keep copies, didn't it? People saved everything else. He typed "old versions of websites" into the search bar, mostly as a joke, and a result came up fast: the Wayback Machine. Carter leaned in as Logan tapped it. The page explained that since 1996 the Internet Archive had been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone could look at old versions of many sites. Logan read the line twice. "Since 1996," he said out loud. "That's older than us."

"Wait, so it's like a museum?" Carter asked.

"It's a machine," Logan said. "The Wayback Machine." He pasted the dead address into the search box and held his breath.

The screen flickered, and there it was: the sixth-grade blog, luminous green and orange, exactly as it had looked three years ago. The class photo at the top showed all of them grinning outside the gym. Logan scrolled, and his stomach tightened. Their teacher, Mr. Nowak, had let everyone sign posts with first names, which seemed fine back then. But under the About section, someone, probably Pedro, had listed the school's cross-country meet schedule with the park addresses. And in the comments, kids had written things like "meet me at the field at 4" with their full names attached.

"Pedro put our whole meet schedule on here," Logan said quietly. "Dates, parks, everything."

Carter set down his granola bar. "Anyone in the world could see when and where we'd be?"

Logan tested it, because guessing wasn't enough. He opened a different tab and searched one of the park names plus the date. The archived page came up in the results, sitting there in the open, no password, no login. A stranger's screenshot of it had even been reposted on a running forum with a comment that said, "Nice group of kids." Logan's arms prickled. He closed the tab.

"So the five dollars," Carter started.

"Excluded," Logan said. "You said the page was gone forever. It's not gone. That's the whole point." He was already drafting a message to Mr. Nowak with the link, asking if the school could ask to have the copies taken down. Then he found his own old essay, the one where he'd predicted everyone would have robot tutors by 2020, and laughed so hard Carter snatched the phone to read it himself.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a flat horizontal line means the object is not moving.
story:
Norah lined up her ramp on the gymnasium floor and taped the measuring tape down before anyone could bump it out of place. Her project, "How Fast Does It Roll?", needed a ball, a stopwatch, and a graph, and the judges would come around in twenty minutes. Beside her table, Romeo was still gluing labels onto his poster about which dinosaurs were a herbivore and which preferred meat, and Gurfateh was pacing with a volcano that refused to erupt.

"Trial five," Norah announced. "Romeo, call time." She held the elastic practice ball at the top of the ramp, let go, and Romeo clicked the stopwatch as it crossed each meter mark. She wrote the numbers, then plotted distance against time, dot by dot, on her big graph paper.

The first four trials made a smooth climbing line, but trial five was strange. The dots rose, then ran flat across the page for almost two seconds, then rose again. Norah stared at it. She had not calculated anything wrong; she had checked twice. Her stomach gave a small twist of dread as the principal's footsteps started down the row of tables.

"Wait," Romeo said, leaning over. "This flat part. What happened there?"

Norah looked at the ramp, then at the floor. Two meters down, the tape met a crack in the tiles, and the crack was exactly where the flat stretch began. She rolled the ball again and watched, not the stopwatch, just the ball. It dropped into the crack, wobbled, sat there, then wiggled free and kept rolling.

"It stopped," she said slowly. "That's why the line goes flat. If the ball isn't moving, distance stays the same while time keeps going." She tapped the flat stretch with her pencil.

"Show us," Gurfateh said, abandoning his volcano.

Ms. Kaur arrived at the table just as Norah set up trial six. "Walk me through your graph," she said.

Norah pointed at the climbing dots first. "Here it's rolling. And here," she said, running her pencil along the flat section, "it's not moving." Then she rolled the ball on cue. It hit the crack, sat, popped out, and rolled on, and Romeo called the seconds out loud. When Norah plotted the new dots, the flat stretch appeared in the same place.

"So what's your fix?" Ms. Kaur asked.

Norah slid her ruler across the crack to bridge it and grinned. "Trial seven."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, so a solution at pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one at pH 4.
story:
Nicholas had promised himself he would figure out the mystery liquid before Tessa arrived, but Grandpa's kitchen stubbornly refused to give up its secret. On the counter sat an old jar of pale blue liquid labeled only in Grandpa's shaky handwriting, "For the tomatoes." Litmus paper, a gift from Mr. Campbell the year before, waited in Nicholas's pencil case, along with a chart of the pH scale he had copied off the board at school. He dipped a strip into a splash of the blue liquid in a saucer, held his breath, and watched it turn pink. Acid, then, though a weak one, which gave him an ambiguous answer: plenty of things in a kitchen were weakly acidic, from lemon juice to vinegar to buttermilk. He needed more clues.

Tessa rang the doorbell twenty minutes later, still holding her bike helmet. "Did you solve it?" she asked, leaning over the saucer. Nicholas showed her the chart. "The paper turned pink, so it's on the acid side of the scale. I compared it with vinegar and lemon juice, and the color matched something in between. pH 4, I think, maybe 5." Tessa squinted at the strip. "So it's basically like vinegar, then. pH 3, pH 4, what's the difference? One number."

"That's what Nathanael said at school," Nicholas told her, "and Mr. Campbell just smiled at him." He tapped the chart with two fingers. "Each whole step is ten times as much, so pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4. That's not one number apart. That's like the difference between one marble and ten marbles." Tessa frowned, then counted the steps on the chart with her finger, from 4 down to 3, then 3 down to 2. "So pH 2 would be a hundred times more acidic than ours?"

Nicholas nodded, and a new thought struck him. If the mystery liquid was only a weak acid, it could not be vinegar, which had tested at pH 3 on his earlier try. He lined up three fresh strips, dipped one in lemon juice, one in vinegar, one in the blue liquid, and laid them side by side on a paper towel. The blue liquid's strip turned a clearly softer pink than vinegar's. Buttermilk, he decided, was the best match, and buttermilk meant one thing in Grandpa's kitchen: pancakes for the tomatoes' harvest lunch. "It's a pretend science experiment that's really breakfast," Tessa said, grinning.

They carried the strips and the chart out to the garden, where Grandpa was tying up tomato vines. "Your jar is buttermilk," Nicholas announced, "and Nathanael owes me a cookie, because pH 3 isn't a little more acidic than pH 4. It's ten times more." Grandpa laughed so hard he had to sit down on the step. "You've got it exactly," he said. "Now wash your hands, you two, and hand me that bowl."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
story:
James had the microscope set up on the kitchen table before his backpack was even unpacked. Mr. Guo had lent it to him for the weekend, along with a box of slides, a jar of iodine stain, and one instruction taped to the lid: "Onion first."

George arrived twenty minutes later, still holding his bike helmet. "Did you cut the onion yet?"

"Half of it," James said, pointing to the cutting board. His eyes had watered so much that he'd had to sit back and blink at the ceiling, but it was worth it. With tweezers he had peeled a paper-thin layer of skin from the inside of an onion ring, laid it flat on a slide, and added one drop of stain. He was ready.

He clicked the low-power lens into place, looked through the eyepiece, and nearly knocked the whole thing over. "George. Come here. You can see the cells. They look like bricks in a wall."

George squeezed in beside him. "Whoa. That's radical." He straightened up. "Okay, so what magnification is this? Mr. Guo said we have to write it on our drawings."

"Fifty," George said. "It says ten on the eyepiece, and it says four right on the lens. Ten and four. Forty." He paused, then added, "Maybe fifty with rounding."

James pulled the little instruction card out of the box again and turned it over. On the back, in Mr. Guo's handwriting, was one line: total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power. He read it twice.

"George. It's not ten plus four. It's ten times four. Forty." He said it slowly, because the idea was rearranging itself in his head. "And look, the other lens says forty on it. So if I switch to that one, ten times forty is..." He grabbed his notebook. "Four hundred. Four hundred times."

"That can't be right," George said. "Forty is already a lot. Four hundred, we'd see, like, the inside of the inside."

"Then let's find out." James's dilemma was gone in an instant; there was only one way to settle it. He swung the 40x objective down, careful not to crunch the slide, bent over the eyepiece, and turned the fine focus knob a hair at a time. The blurry grey smear sharpened. Then it snapped into place, and he forgot how to breathe.

Each cell stood out like its own little room, outlined in a thick dark wall, with a stained dot sitting near the middle. "George, I can see the nucleus. And the cell wall, the whole outline. And the membrane, right inside the wall." He drew three quick arrows in his notebook, labeling as fast as he could write.

George took his turn at the eyepiece and was quiet for a long moment. "Okay. Four hundred. You were right." He laughed. "Fifty. I said fifty."

"Don't worry about it," James said, trying to console him, though he was grinning too wide for it to sound sincere. "You want to do the math on the last lens, the one that says ten? Because I'm putting that one on next."

George leaned over the nosepiece and read the tiny number. "Ten times ten. One hundred."

"One hundred it is," James said, and swung the lens into place.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells.
story:
The problem with the onion was not the smell, though Jacob's eyes watered so badly that Jackson had to finish peeling the paper-thin skin for him. The problem was that Jacob could not find the nucleus. Mr. Zhang had drawn three things on the board and told everyone to label them on their slides: the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. Jacob could see the wall, a neat rectangle around each cell like a brick in a wall, and the membrane hugged the inside of it, but the nucleus was supposed to be a dark spot and he saw nothing except pale gray shapes floating in the light of the microscope.

He turned the fine focus knob one click at a time, the way they had been taught, and still nothing. Beside him, Jackson was already labeling his diagram with quick pencil strokes. Florent, whose hair always smelled faintly of vinegar on lab days, leaned over from the next station.

"Mine's there," Florent said. "Little dark blob, right in the middle. Who even noticed that thing first? Somebody had to see it before everyone else, right?" Jacob sat back. That question snagged in his mind the way the onion skin had snagged on the tweezers. Whoever it was must have looked at thousands of cells and picked out one small dot that could have been dirt, or a shadow, or nothing at all.

Then Jacob had an idea. Maybe his spot was not in the middle of the cell. Maybe it was hiding near the wall, thin and pale, the way the membrane was, and he had skimmed past it. He decided to test it. He stopped sweeping his eyes across the whole slide and instead examined each cell like he was checking lockers for a lost glove, edge to edge, one cell at a time. He started at the top left and worked down in rows, slowly, refusing to skip anything.

In the second row, fourth cell from the right, he found it: a small, dense circle pressed close to the wall, so faint he had dismissed it twice already. He hunched over the eyepiece and grinned. "Found it. It was hanging out by the wall like a koala in a pouch." Florent laughed. "That's the most marsupial thing you've ever said." Down the row, Jackson looked up from his diagram, where he had carefully nurtured each letter of his labels so the ink would not smear, as if neat handwriting could make him immune to a bad grade.

Mr. Zhang stopped at their station and asked who could tell him about that dark spot. Florent raised his hand. "It was Robert Brown, a Scottish botanist. He described the nucleus in 1831, studying orchid cells." Mr. Zhang nodded and moved on, and Jacob wrote the three labels on his own diagram, pressing hard enough that the word nucleus showed through onto the next page. At the bottom of his paper he added one more line, small, just for himself: fourth cell from the right.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a line that curves upward and gets steeper shows an object speeding up.
story:
Nathan dragged the broom handle into the kitchen and propped one end on a stack of cookbooks, making a ramp that ran down to the tile floor. Science was due first period tomorrow, and Mr. Friedman had been clear: no graph, no grade. The assignment said to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time, then draw a distance-time graph. Nathan had a marble, a stopwatch app, and a friend on video call.

"Did you mark the floor yet?" Malory asked from the tablet propped against the fruit bowl. Her dad was a contractor, so she had insisted on the tape measure. Nathan crouched and stuck strips of masking tape every thirty centimetres, all the way to the refrigerator.

"Not in vain, I hope," he said, sitting back on his heels. "If this marble stops rolling halfway, I'm taping a bigger slope."

They ran the marble ten times. Nathan called out the times as it crossed each strip, and Malory read them back so he could write them down. At thirty centimetres it took almost a second. At the last strip, three metres away, it crossed in barely more than another. He plotted the points on graph paper, expecting a straight line, because straight lines were what he knew how to handle.

The points climbed into a curve. At the start the line rose slowly, almost flat, and then it bent upward, steeper and steeper toward the corner of the page. Nathan stared at it, tapping his pencil. He had assumed the marble rolled at one steady speed, but that would have made a straight line, and this was nothing like one. The steep part matched where the marble had blazed across the last strips of tape. He grabbed a fresh sheet and tried a gentle ramp made from a cereal box, and this time the curve barely bent. "It's not an illusion," he told Malory, holding the two graphs side by side for the camera. "The line curves upward and gets steeper when the ball is speeding up. Steeper ramp, faster marble, curvier line."

"Then do the big one again with the golf ball," Malory said. "Mr. Friedman loves a second trial."

Nathan fetched the golf ball from the garage, set it at the top of the broom handle, and clicked the stopwatch with his thumb. "Three, two, one, roll."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Clay pieces must be completely dry before they are fired in a kiln, because leftover water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece.
story:
Andrew had spent two whole Saturdays shaping a clay Tyrannosaurus rex in Mr. Luo's backyard studio, and today was firing day. The art teacher at school had assigned a project on extinction, and Andrew figured a T-rex would be the most influential example anyone could pick, since everybody knew what had happened to the dinosaurs. Mr. Luo had agreed to fire the pieces in his kiln, so Andrew carried his dinosaur over in a shoebox, walking carefully so the tiny arms would not snap off.

Teagan was already there with her clay bowl, and Philip had made a lopsided volcano. Mr. Luo lined the pieces up on the bench beside the kiln, then picked up each one and pressed his palm against it. "This one's fine," he said, setting down Teagan's bowl. "This one, too." When he reached Andrew's dinosaur, he paused. "Still damp. It waits."

"But it feels dry," Andrew said, running his finger along the T-rex's back.

Mr. Luo just shook his head and placed the dinosaur at the far end of the bench. "I don't permit damp clay in the kiln." That was all he said, which meant Andrew had to figure out the rest himself.

While Mr. Luo loaded the kiln, Andrew studied his dinosaur. The surface looked exactly as dry as Teagan's bowl. He touched his own cheek, then the clay, then his cheek again. The clay felt cooler, the way a sidewalk feels cool in the evening even after a hot day. Somewhere inside that coolness, he realized, there had to be water he could not see, hiding under the surface where his eyes were useless.

Teagan leaned over. "Maybe you could dry it faster," she suggested. Philip pointed at the kiln. "Put it on top. That thing gets hot." Andrew glanced at Mr. Luo, who was busy stacking shelves and did not object, so he set the shoebox on the warm metal lid of the closed kiln. It was like a low stove, not hot enough to do anything sudden, just gently warm. He turned the dinosaur every ten minutes so no side would stay hidden against the box.

"Why does it matter, though?" Philip asked. "If it's a little wet, so what?"

Andrew thought about the kettle in his kitchen, the way water disappears into a puff when it boils. "Mr. Luo said water trapped inside turns to steam, and steam can crack the piece. Or burst it." Philip winced, imagining his volcano blowing up for real.

After an hour, Andrew pressed his palm against the T-rex the way he had seen Mr. Luo do. The clay felt warm all the way through, the same temperature as the kiln lid, with no cool spot anywhere. He carried it over. "Could you check it now?"

Mr. Luo held it, tapped it once with his knuckle, and nodded. "Bone dry. In it goes." He opened the kiln, and Andrew watched his dinosaur disappear onto the shelf beside Teagan's bowl, right before the heavy door clanged shut.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
story:
Olivier had exactly one goal for the field trip to the science center: beat Calum in the exhibit challenge. Each student got a card with questions, and the first to finish won a free pass for the planetarium. Calum had won the last two class competitions, and his smirk about it was getting unbearable.

The trouble started at the "Inside Animals" hall, where a keeper was walking a actual cow past a pen of hay. Question eleven read: "Watch the cow for one full minute. What is it doing, and why?" The cow stood there chewing, its jaw swinging side to side, though it hadn't taken a single bite of anything new for the whole time Olivier watched. "It's bored," Calum said, writing fast. "Cows just chew when they're bored." That sounded like an assumption, not an answer, and Olivier said so. Calum shrugged and moved on, eager to acquire his planetarium pass.

Anais crouched near the rail with her camera. She needed a good animal photo for her art project, and she kept waiting for the cow to do something interesting. "Chewing isn't interesting," she muttered. Olivier was skeptical of that too. Something about the rhythm bothered him. The cow would swallow, pause, then a lump would travel up its neck and the chewing would start again, slow and even, like a machine on a timer.

He followed the lump with his eyes and wandered to the glass case behind the pen. Inside sat a huge model of a cow's stomach, split open into four compartments, each one labeled. The first was the biggest, marked "rumen," and next to it a magnified panel showed tiny specks squirming inside. "Microbes," the small caption read, "that help break down tough grass stored in the rumen." Beside the case, a kid from another school was reading aloud to his friend: "The cow brings that grass back up and chews it again as cud."

Olivier stood very still, watching the lump rise up the cow's neck one more time. It was bringing grass back up. It wasn't bored at all. It was doing the second half of a job, right there in front of everyone. He wrote his answer, then leaned toward the rail and pointed at the cow's neck. "Anais, film right there. Something's coming up." She raised her camera just as the lump traveled up, and the cow's jaw began its slow swing again. "Got it," she whispered.

Calum came back scowling, holding his card against the light. "The keeper says the bored answer is wrong. There's some word I missed." "Cud," Olivier said. "And the first stomach part is called the rumen." He was still two questions behind, and the planetarium pass was far from won, but Anais turned her camera screen toward both of them. "Look at this," she said. "Best picture I've taken all year."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Joining a club or team at a new school puts a student in regular contact with the same people who share an interest, which gives friendships time to grow.
story:
The moving van turned out of the driveway, and Alyssa's dad pulled the family car in behind it. Alyssa sat in the back with her knees pressed against the seat in front of her. In her lap she held a shoebox of things she refused to let the movers touch: a fossil she'd found at camp, a photo of her and Celine at the lake, and the small chess set Aryana had given her at last week's going-away party.

"Two hundred miles to Riverside," her dad said, glancing at the mirror. "Plenty of time to make a plan."

Alyssa didn't answer. She was thinking about Celine and Aryana, who had known her since kindergarten, and about how at Riverside Middle she would know exactly nobody. She stared out the window at a strip of shops sliding past, one with a neon sign that seemed to radiate pink light even in the morning sun.

She remembered the start of sixth grade, when Aryana had joined the art club. Before that, Aryana had been just a girl from Alyssa's math class whose name she sometimes mixed up. But art club met every Tuesday after school, the same kids every time, all of them drawing the same bowls of fruit. Somewhere between the second Tuesday and the tenth, Aryana and Alyssa had gone from classmates to inseparable. Alyssa could still picture Aryana laughing so hard at a lopsided pear that she'd knocked over her water cup.

Alyssa sat up straighter in the back seat. It hadn't been luck, she realized. Aryana and she had seen each other again and again, all year, doing something they both liked. That was how their friendship had actually been built, Tuesday by Tuesday, like the layers of sediment in her fossil. A whole school was too big to find friends in. But a club, one small group that met regularly?

"Dad, does the school have clubs?"

"Check the folder on the seat," he said. "It's the paperwork from the district."

Alyssa dug through the folder while the highway hummed beneath the tires. Band, robotics, gardening, chess. Her heart dipped a little at gardening, which she'd loved at her old school, where she and Celine had planted flowers to attract butterflies and watched the hummingbirds steal nectar from the trumpet vines. But she'd never played chess with anyone except her grandfather, two summers ago, and she'd mostly lost.

She kept reading anyway. The chess club met twice a week at lunch. Lunch. That meant the members would be eating together in the same room, over the same boards, with plenty of time to talk. Regular contact, same people, shared interest. She tested the idea against what she knew. Aryana and art club: fit perfectly. Celine and soccer team: fit too, every practice, same girls, one ball. Even her parents had met at a weekly bowling league, not by some one-time accident in a supermarket line.

"I'm going to join the chess club," Alyssa announced.

"You don't really play," her dad said.

"I know. But I want somewhere to go at lunch, and I'll learn." She took out a pen and wrote her name on the sign-up form, pressing hard enough that she could feel the letters through the paper. It didn't feel like a promise exactly, but it wasn't nothing either. Nothing at the new school would be permanent yet, and maybe that was the good part.

Near the edge of Riverside, they passed a school with a marquee that read welcome students, clubs open next week. Alyssa opened the shoebox, set the chess set on top of the photo, and positioned the white queen on its square, ready for a first move.

"Two hundred miles behind us," her dad said as the moving van signaled toward their new street.

"Queen to e4," Alyssa said.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Lucas flopped into the desk chair and pulled up the group chat for the science project. Three messages sat there from Axl: "did you finish the graph," "hello??," and then, in huge letters, "WHERE ARE YOU." Before Lucas could type anything, Graydon had already replied, "why are you yelling?" Lucas frowned at the screen. Axl wasn't angry as far as he knew, so why did the whole chat feel like a fire alarm had gone off?

He tried an experiment. He typed "sorry, dinner ran late" in normal letters, then sent a second message the same words but in all capitals, just to himself in a private notes tab where nobody else could see it. The identical sentence somehow felt different on his own screen, like it had jumped three feet closer to his face. On a page in his notebook he tried to isolate what had changed. Same words, same order, same kid typing them. The only difference was the size of the letters.

"It's the caps," he muttered. He opened a chat with Graydon alone, which felt quieter, almost like talking in a hallway instead of the middle of the cafeteria. "do you read all caps as shouting?" he typed. Graydon answered in seconds: "yeah, everybody does. axl just does it when he wants to be noticed." Lucas leaned back. So there was a rule hiding inside the chat, an unwritten one, and it worked the same for other people as it did for him.

His objective for the project was still to finish the graph before Friday, so he went back to the group chat and typed, "graph is half done. axl, we still need your data on the crickets." Then, remembering his experiment, he added a line in capital letters: "SEND THE CRICKET NUMBERS TONIGHT." Axl replied instantly, "ok ok, geez, no need to shout." Lucas grinned. The rule worked in both directions.

Axl's data arrived twenty minutes later, messy but complete. Lucas sorted the numbers while Graydon cleaned up the graph labels, and by the time Lucas's mom knocked on the door to say lights out soon, the chart looked almost finished. It had taken a few tries, and one accidental yell, but the adaptation felt easy now: big letters when something mattered, small letters for everything else. Axl sent one last message, all in caps: "WE ARE GOING TO GET AN A." Lucas laughed and typed back, "why are you yelling?"

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
story:
Cooper stood at the kitchen counter with a printout of the Japji Sahib in front of him and a bowl of flour his mother had left for the rotis. The ceremony was in three weeks, and his grandmother had said he must know the whole morning prayer by heart. Mandatory, she had said, not as a suggestion but as a fact. He had tried reciting it eleven times since breakfast, and every time he lost his place around the same line, like a stair that was missing in a staircase.
