His friend Mara came over after school and sat on the counter stool, eating the crackers he was supposed to be saving. "Say it again," she said. "I'll follow on your printout." He got through the beginning, stumbled, and stopped. She slid the paper across. "Look. You always trip here. But the line before it, you know cold. So it's not the hard line that's the problem. It's that you're relying on the words coming in a rush, and when they don't coincide with what your mouth expects, you stall."

Cooper thought about that. The rhythm, not the words, was breaking. He tested it. He clapped a slow beat on the counter, one clap per line, and recited with the claps. The claps forced his mouth to wait, and the hard line arrived on its own beat instead of collapsing into the line before it. He got through it once, all the way. He tried again without clapping, keeping the beat in his head. It held.

"Why does it have to be this one anyway?" Mara asked. "You know lots of prayers."

"It's the Amrit Sanchar," Cooper said. "That's what the ceremony is called. It's the Khalsa initiation. The Japji Sahib gets recited there, so it's not just any prayer." He hadn't known that himself until Tuesday, when he'd found his grandfather's old booklet and the page about the ceremony folded into it. He had asked one question at dinner and his grandmother had answered with one sentence and then gone back to eating, which was how she gave the most important information.

He recited it again, slower, and the missing stair was there now, a real step he could stand on. Mara stole another cracker. His mother came in, tied her apron, and pointed at the flour he still hadn't touched. "Rotis," she said. "Your part of the deal." Cooper picked up the dough and kept the beat going under his breath while he rolled it flat, one line for each round of the pin.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, making it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports.
story:
The living room smelled like popcorn and melted cheese, and every seat was taken ten minutes before the puck dropped. Alice sat cross-legged on the floor between Javier and Matthias, while her dad and the neighbour, Ms. Pham, claimed the couch. On the screen, the arena lights blazed, and the commentators kept showing a close-up of the big silver trophy with its dents and scratches and bands covered in names.

"Why does it look so beat up?" Javier asked, pointing his popcorn at the screen. "Couldn't they polish it or get a new one?"

"It looks ancient," Matthias said. "My dad says they make new trophies for every other sport. Why is hockey stuck with this crumbly old thing?"

Alice leaned closer to the screen, squinting at the trophy's worn surface. "I don't presume they're too cheap to buy a new one," she said slowly. "There has to be a reason they keep using this exact one. Something about it must matter more than looking shiny."

"Two minutes until the second period," her dad warned, checking his phone. "Whatever you're doing, do it fast."

Alice grabbed the tablet from the side table and started typing, her fingers flying. The crowd on TV roared through a commercial break, and Matthias kept glancing between her search and the clock, bouncing his knees. "Hurry, hurry," he chanted.

"Wait, wait, I've got it," Alice said. She read fast, then looked up with her eyes wide. "It's old because it's actually old. For real. It was donated by Lord Stanley, who was Canada's governor general, in 1892, and first awarded in 1893. That makes it the oldest trophy in all of North American professional sports. It's not supposed to look new. It's been around longer than any other trophy, longer than grandparents, longer than cars even."

"Eighteen ninety-two?" Ms. Pham repeated, leaning forward. "That's why it looks like that. It's not worn out, it's historic."

"Every dent is from a whole different team, ages ago," Javier said, staring at the screen like he was seeing the trophy for the first time. "I thought it was just dented. I changed my mind. It's the best-looking trophy in sports."

Matthias had been rooting for the far-away team all series, but he nudged Alice's shoulder. "Okay, your team's trophy is cooler. Mine can still win it, though."

"If they win tonight," Alice said, "they'll be the ones scratching new names onto a hundred-year-old cup. That's the whole point."

The horn sounded for the second period, and the room erupted into shouting. Matthias grabbed a cushion, Alice jumped to her feet, and Ms. Pham covered her eyes. The dented old trophy gleamed on the screen one last time before the puck dropped.

"Faceoff!" Alice shouted.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Average speed equals distance travelled divided by the time taken.
story:
Jack had taped a chalk line across the patio and marked off five metres with his dad's old tape measure, one chalk tick for every metre. Marcus sat on the overturned wheelbarrow with his phone, stopwatch ready.

"Grayson says his marble is faster than both of ours," Marcus said. "But he rolled his on his driveway, which is downhill. He's just going to keep saying he won."

"It isn't a race unless everyone rolls on the same track," Jack said. He crouched at the chalk line and set his marble, the green one with the swirl, behind his thumb. "But even here, every roll comes out different. My thumb pushes harder some times."

"So how do you know which marble is actually fastest?"

Jack thought about that while he flicked the marble. It clicked along the patio stones, wobbled at the third metre, and crossed the last chalk tick while Marcus called out the time. They wrote it on the clipboard: 5 metres, 4.1 seconds. They rolled again. 4.3. Again. 4.0.

From the other side of the fence, Ms. Mercado looked over from her tomato plants. "Science in progress over there?"

"Trying to find out which marble is really fastest," Jack said.

"Are you timing a single run, or are you dividing?" she asked, and went back to her tomatoes before he could answer.

Jack stared at the clipboard. Five metres, four seconds one time, four seconds three tenths the next. He pencilled it out: 5 divided by 4.1. 5 divided by 4.3. 5 divided by 4.0. The answers came out close, all around 1.2. "Marcus, look. Average speed. You take the distance travelled and divide it by the time taken."

"That's it? That easy?"

"That's the formula, and it's fair, because we can do the exact same math for Grayson's marble if he rolls it here on flat ground." Jack drew a quick graph in the corner of the page, distance up the side, time along the bottom, and plotted their three points. They sat almost in a straight line. "And look at that. The line means it's not just luck. The marble keeps close to the same speed the whole way."

Marcus rolled his marble next, the blue one with the frost inside, and Jack timed it: 5 metres, 3.6 seconds. 5 divided by 3.6 came out to about 1.4, faster than Jack's 1.2. Jack laughed and pushed the clipboard across the wheelbarrow. "Ironic. I built the whole track and your marble beats mine by a mile."

"We could retire the green one," Marcus said, and Jack shook his head, picked it up, and set it behind his thumb for one more roll.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
story:
The quarry had filled with rainwater years ago, and now the town ran a swim dock there from June through August, so Aurora had grown up hearing that the water was her family's heritage. Her grandfather had cut stone out of this pit before it flooded. Today she sat on the flat top of a granite block with Nancy and Carly, all three of them still damp, their orange life vests folded beside them, and none of them thinking about geology. They were thinking about the science test on Monday.

"I keep getting it wrong," Carly said, poking a stick into the gravel. "Ms. Campbell asked why we have summer, and I said we're closer to the Sun. She said half the class said that too, and it's not it."

Aurora exhaled slowly and squinted across the pale water. She had said the same thing herself on Thursday, and it had bothered her all weekend. If distance wasn't the answer, something else had to be. She turned her flashlight over in her hands, the one she'd brought because the three of them had planned to walk the far path home in the dusk, and then she looked at the round white bucket Nancy was carrying.

"Can I borrow that?" Aurora said. She set the bucket on the granite, held her flashlight a step away, and clicked it on. "Okay, this is the Sun. The bucket is Earth. Watch."

She moved the bucket in a slow circle around the flashlight. "The axis," she said, mostly to herself, "the line through the middle. Is it straight up and down, or is it leaning?" She remembered the old globe in the library, the one with the bent metal rod through it, and how she'd always assumed somebody had dented it. Her hand steadied the bucket at a tilt, top tipped away, and she carried it around the light again, keeping the lean pointed the same way the whole trip. At one side of the circle the tipped top aimed toward the flashlight; at the other side it aimed away.

"Summer," Nancy said slowly, watching the lit side, "and then winter." She grabbed the bucket herself and walked it around again, and her eyes went wide. "And it's tilted the whole time, like it's pinned."

"How much?" Carly asked.

Aurora thought of the globe again, the little printed number on its stand. "About 23.4 degrees from straight up," she said, "compared with the flat ring of its orbit around the Sun." She tipped the bucket to show the angle, not too much, not too little.

"That's so weird," Carly said, but she was grinning now, and she pulled the life vest back on even though they weren't going near the water again. "Okay, walk it around once more."

Aurora carried the bucket through its slow circle, flashlight steady, the tilted top swinging toward the light and away and back again, while the last swimmers climbed the dock ladder behind them and the water went gold.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The simple interest formula is I = P x r x t: interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years.
story:
Mason had a system for his paycheques from the garden centre: forty dollars every second Saturday, filed into an envelope marked with a felt pen that was starting to run dry. He had the system because Ms. Pham, the owner, kept a rack of bank brochures by the register, and customers read them while waiting for their tulip bulbs. One slow Tuesday, a random orange pamphlet fell out of the rack, and Mason picked it up mostly because it had fallen on the petunias.

The pamphlet showed a savings account. Two accounts, actually, side by side. Gracelynn, who also worked Tuesdesdays and who was saving for concert tickets, leaned over his shoulder. "Which one pays more?"

"That's the thing," Mason said. "It doesn't exactly say. It gives a formula." He read it aloud, slowly, because it looked like something invented to punish people. "I equals P times r times t. Interest equals principal times the yearly rate times the number of years. It's called simple interest."

"Sounds simple if you say it fast," Gracelynn said, and went back to repricing the terracotta pots, which she did with great authority for someone saving for concert tickets.

Mason found a pencil behind the register. He wrote P at the top, then picked a number he could actually imagine: one hundred dollars. The rate in the pamphlet was five percent, and the other account showed five years, so he multiplied. One hundred times five percent gave five dollars a year, and five years of that gave twenty-five dollars. Simple interest, twenty-five dollars. The other account, the one with no formula at all, just a small table, showed a bigger number for the same hundred dollars over the same five years. Not much bigger. Annoyingly bigger.

"Gracelynn, look at this." She came over, wiping pot dust on her jeans. He showed her his pencil work. "Twenty-five from the formula. The table says more. The table's for compound interest. It pays interest on the interest."

"That sounds made up," she said. "Banks don't just give you extra money for nothing." She squinted at the table, then at his arithmetic, then checked his multiplication twice, which was more checking than she had ever done on anything at school. When she got the same twenty-five, she frowned at the compound column like it had insulted her mother. "Okay," she said finally. "Okay, so the compound one is more, and the more years, the more it wins?"

He tried to articulate why that would be true, that each year's interest sat on top of the last year's interest, so there was always a slightly bigger pile being multiplied, but he mostly ended up drawing a lopsided stack of boxes. Gracelynn tapped the drawing anyway. "You're like the protagonist of a math movie," she said. "Fine. New plan. Concert tickets, then whatever's left goes into the compound one. The boring orange one."

She took the pamphlet home. Mason wrote one hundred dollars on a fresh envelope, then put it in the drawer under the register, next to the felt pen.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
story:
The number 42 bus was packed, and Alexia had to stand, gripping the pole while her library books slid around inside her backpack. She was on her way to Susie's house to finish their history project on wartime posters, and in her notebook was the best thing she had found all week. Back in 1937, a group called the Institute for Propaganda Analysis had been founded in the United States, right there in her library book, and its whole purpose was to teach ordinary people how to recognize propaganda.

"Guess what I found," she said, when Susie and Paxton squeezed onto the bus at the next stop.

"You finally confessed to eating my fruit snacks in third grade?" Paxton said.

"Better." She held up her notebook. "In 1937, in the United States, they founded the Institute for Propaganda Analysis. It taught regular people to spot propaganda tricks. And I think the tricks are still everywhere. Look." She pointed at the ad above the seats. A smiling movie star held a bottle of soda, with the words THE DRINK EVERYONE LOVES in giant letters. "That's a celebrity testimonial. And 'everyone loves' is a bandwagon appeal. They want you to feel left out if you don't buy it."

Susie squinted at it. "I never noticed that before."

"That's the whole point," Alexia said. "The tricks work best when you don't see them, like erosion. You don't watch a hillside wear away, but one day there's a valley." She had learned that word in science and liked how it fit. "So here's my test. I bet we can find at least five tricks before we get off at Marsh Street."

They started counting. A poster for a mayoral candidate called his opponent "a reckless schemer," which Alexia flagged as loaded words, designed to make listeners feel something before they could think. A gym ad shouted JOIN THOUSANDS ALREADY GETTING FIT. A bank poster showed a famous quarterback. Paxton spotted the sixth one himself, an ad for a new phone that called every other brand "sad and outdated."

"Okay, you win," Susie said, laughing. "But what does this have to do with our poster project?"

"Everything. Our posters are from the war years, and they use the same stuff. Everyone is doing their part. Loose lips sink ships. It's bandwagon and loaded words, just older." Alexia flipped to a photo of a poster showing a determined factory worker. "The institute would have called this one out in a second."

Paxton leaned against the pole, thinking. "So people back then were learning to see through it? Regular people on a bus, like us?"

"Exactly like us," Alexia said.

The bus shuddered to a stop at Marsh Street, and an older woman near the door struggled with two heavy grocery bags. Susie grabbed one without being asked, and Alexia steadied the woman's elbow as they stepped down onto the hot, arid sidewalk, where the afternoon sun had baked the concrete pale.

"Project's going to be amazing," Paxton said, squinting up at the bus as it pulled away, every one of its ads still glowing with promises.

Alexia watched it go. "As long as we write this part in," she said. "All of it. Starting with 1937."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Lowering the coverslip onto the slide at an angle, one edge first, helps push out air so fewer bubbles form over the cells.
story:
Ryan crouched beside the fallen log on the nature trail, tweezers in one hand and a paper bag in the other. Their science class had hiked out here with portable microscopes so they could prepare slides in the field, and Mr. Byrne had promised that anyone who drew a properly labelled onion cell drawing would get extra credit. Ryan wanted that credit, but mostly he wanted to see the cells himself, the real striped bricks under the skin of an onion they'd brought from home. He peeled off the papery outer layer and teased a thin, clear square of the inner skin onto his glass slide.

Kohen set up the little microscope on a flat rock while Chase dropped to one knee beside him, wincing. A branch had whipped back and scratched his leg on the way in, and he kept glancing at it. "My mom says scratches like that can get an infection if you don't wash them," he said. Mr. Byrne dug a wipe out of the first aid kit and handed it over without a word, and Chase cleaned the red line and seemed to relax.

The real trouble started with the drop of iodine and the coverslip. Ryan lowered the thin square of glass straight down onto his specimen, flat, all at once. When he looked through the eyepiece, the whole field was crowded with round circles, dark-ringed and smug, and not a single one had a nucleus. "Those are cells," Kohen said, leaning in after him. "Weird ones." Ryan frowned. They didn't look like the diagram in the textbook. The circles were perfectly round, some of them big, some small, and they were everywhere. He rotated the focus knob and the circles didn't sharpen into walls or membranes, just stayed rimmed in black.

He sat back and thought about it. His teacher had told them air could ruin a slide, and it clicked. He tested a simple idea: start over, and change only one thing, the way the coverslip went down. This time he touched one edge of the coverslip to the iodine first, then lowered the rest slowly at an angle, letting the edge lead the way across. When he bent to the eyepiece, the field was nearly clear of circles. Laid out before him were the brick-like cells, each one bordered, each with a dense dot near the middle. "Look at this," he said, and Chase and Kohen crowded in, bumping shoulders.

"So those round things before," Chase said slowly, "were just air bubbles?" He'd been insisting they were cells a minute ago, and now he shook his head at himself. "I was wrong." Ryan grinned and started his drawing, labelling the outer wall of each brick, then the thin line just inside it, then the nucleus, checking each label against the field guide page. The first slide had taught him something even though it had failed. He persevered through two more slides, and each one came out cleaner, the bubbles fewer and fewer, the cells plainer.

By the time they hiked back toward the trailhead, Ryan had a finished drawing in his bag and iodine stains on his fingers. "Same time next week?" Kohen asked, swinging his backpack onto his shoulders. Ryan held up the drawing so the sunlight shone through the paper. "Bring two onions," he said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
story:
Jace followed his mother through the doors of the cultural center carrying a box of marigolds, the paper of the crate warm against his chest. Mr. McKenzie met them near the back hall, where tables had been pushed together into a long altar already crowded with candles, bread, and cut-out papel picado strung overhead. "Jace, good, you're here," Mr. McKenzie said. "Your class is setting up the display for the celebration tonight. Rae and Livia are already arguing about the top shelf."

They were. Rae held a framed photograph of a man in a wide-brimmed hat, and Livia had her hands on the frame too. "It goes in the middle," Rae insisted. "He's my great-grandfather, and this is the most important spot." Livia shook her head. "There's no most important spot. Look at the picture my mom printed for the flyer. People build these at home, in their houses, and everything on them means something to the family, not to strangers." She tugged gently, and the frame tipped, and Jace caught it before it hit the table.

Later, while the others draped purple cloth, Jace studied the altar and tried to work out the rule behind it. The photo Rae had added, the little dish of peanuts, a plastic violin, someone's favorite candy. He noticed the pattern: every object seemed to belong to one person who had died, as if each little grouping said a name. Then he remembered his grandfather, gone since March, and his stomach dropped. His mother had left his grandfather's harmonica in the car, but there was no photograph of him in the box at all. If each section belonged to someone, then an empty spot with only a harmonica might mean nothing.

He decided to test the idea. He asked Rae, "Why the photo? Would the peanuts work alone?" She gave him a look. "The food was his favorite, but the photo is him. My abuela says the ofrenda welcomes him home. It's a ritual, like a door opening. November first and second, that's when we do it, and everything on the altar is for the people in our family who died." Jace nodded slowly. If the photo was the door, then he needed one, and it needed to be his.

He borrowed Mr. McKenzie's phone and messaged his mother: "Can you send the picture of Abuelo from the hallway? The one with the fishing boat." Her reply came in two minutes, a photo of his grandfather squinting into the sun, laughing at something off camera. Mr. McKenzie printed it on the office printer, and Jace set it beside the harmonica with the marigolds circling both.

Rae stood beside him, arms crossed, watching the candles being lit for the crowd that would arrive within the hour, the celebration imminent. "You didn't know you needed the picture," she said, "and you figured it out anyway. That's the point, I think. My great-grandfather would like your grandfather. They both look like trouble." Jace put the harmonica to his lips and blew one wobbly note over the ofrenda, and somewhere in the crowd his mother's hands started clapping.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: People with age-related hearing loss find it especially hard to follow speech when there is background noise.
story:
On Monday morning, Aurora's grandmother arrived with one small suitcase and a promise to stay exactly one week. At dinner that first night, Grandmother laughed at Aurora's story about Zain's runaway science fair volcano and asked sensible questions about Aurora's teachers, including Ms. Suryanto, who apparently taught chemistry to Aurora's mother thirty years ago. Conversations at home were easy. Grandmother caught every word, even when Aurora mumbled into her noodles.

The trouble started Wednesday at the train station. Aurora and her grandmother went to meet Samira arriving from the city, and the station was roaring: announcements crackling overhead, a coffee machine hissing, dozens of strangers talking at once. Aurora said, "The platform number changed," and Grandmother smiled and nodded and then walked toward the wrong platform. Aurora had to jog after her, tug her sleeve, and shout it twice. Later, at a crowded food stall, Grandmother answered a question Aurora hadn't asked. Something was wrong, and Aurora wanted to know what, because at home there had been nothing wrong at all.

She decided to run a test, the way Ms. Suryanto would have wanted. Thursday evening, with only the hum of the refrigerator behind them, she whispered, "Do you want tea?" Grandmother heard it instantly. Friday morning, with the radio on and the blender grinding, she asked the same question at normal volume, and Grandmother tilted her head and said, "Purple?" That was the pattern. The problem wasn't the words themselves. It was the noise underneath them. Grandmother's hearing worked best in quiet and fell apart when the room got loud, something Aurora suspected was true for many older ears, not just her grandmother's.

On Saturday, the last full day, the air turned humid and heavy, and a storm rolled in over the neighborhood. Thunder boomed, rain drummed the roof, and the living room filled with a roar of sound. Grandmother was mid-story about a flooded market in her old town, and Aurora watched her falter, frowning at the noise as if it had swallowed her sentences. Instead of raising her voice and adding to the din, Aurora did the opposite. She walked over, sat close, and turned the fan and the television off. "Sorry," she said. "Too loud in here."

Grandmother picked up her story exactly where she'd left off, and this time not a word escaped. When Samira and Zain came over to say goodbye to the guest, Aurora steered everyone to the quiet back porch, away from the kitchen clatter, and Grandmother followed every joke, even the quiet ones.

Sunday came too fast. At the door, Grandmother squeezed Aurora's hand and said, "You never once made me feel like I'd failed a hearing test." Aurora had privately wanted to resign herself to shouting for the rest of the visit, but she was glad she hadn't. "Come back soon," she said, "and we'll pick the quiet seats." Grandmother winked, picked up her small suitcase, and stepped into the soft grey morning.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Each operation has an inverse that undoes it: subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
story:
Logan stared at the paper on the kitchen table like it had insulted him. Tomorrow morning, first period, Ms. He was giving a quiz, and right there in problem three sat x + 7 = 12, smug and unsolvable. He tapped his pencil, got up, checked the clock, and sat back down. Two hours until bedtime. That was the deadline, and the x was winning.

His phone buzzed beside his milk glass. It was a text from Khalid: "Stuck on the quiz review? Same. x + 7 = 12 is impossible. I asked Zoelie and she just wrote back, 'What undoes adding?' and I still don't get it." Logan read it twice. Undoes? You couldn't undo a plus. It wasn't a shoelace. He typed back "no idea" and set the phone down, but the word stuck to him like gum on a shoe.

He tried Zoelie's idea anyway, just to prove it was nonsense. If x plus 7 made 12, then the x was hiding under there somewhere, like a wrapped present. He couldn't see it, but he could test something. What if he took 7 away from the 12? Twelve minus 7 was 5. So maybe x was 5. He checked it, heart thumping: 5 plus 7 really did equal 12. It worked. Subtraction undoes addition, he scribbled in the margin, feeling like he'd found a secret trapdoor. He grabbed the phone. "KHALID. Subtract the 7 from the other side. It's called the inverse. Then check it." The reply came fast: "WAIT. It works. I got 5 too. Is every problem like this?"

Logan's eyes ran down the page and stopped at 3x = 15. Different beast. There was no plus to undo, so he almost texted Khalid that this one was truly impossible, but then he thought about the pattern. If taking away undoes adding, then something must undo multiplying. He tried dividing. Fifteen divided by 3 was 5, and 3 times 5 really did equal 15. Both answers were 5, and both checked out, which meant the two equations were equivalent, two doors into the same room. He changed his mind about giving up and flipped the paper over instead, hunting for more.

He worked the next four problems without stopping, doing the same thing to both sides every time and watching his answers check out like clockwork. His mom passed through and paused to monitor his progress from the doorway, saying only, "Looks serious." He held up the page. "Inverse operations," he said. "Quiz tomorrow. I'm going to ace it." Then problem nine caught his eye, and he pulled the paper back and picked up his pencil.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime checker must handle numbers below 2 separately, because 0, 1 and negative numbers are not prime, yet a divisor loop starting at 2 finds nothing to reject them.
story:
Ryan's whole plan for the computer lab was to finish before Grady, who sat one seat over and had already typed four lines while Ryan was still finding the number keys. "Mr. Yilmaz said the program has to say if a number is prime," Ryan muttered. "Prime means nothing divides it except one and itself." Grady nodded without looking up, which Ryan took as permission to stop talking.

He wrote his loop so it tried every divisor starting at 2, and if none of them worked, it printed "prime." He typed 7 and got prime. He typed 9 and got "not prime," which smelled like victory. Then he typed 0, just to be safe, because Grady had typed 0 and crashed his own program with an error that made the screen flash red like a fire alarm.

Ryan's program did not crash. It said, in tidy white letters, "0 is prime."

"That's wrong," Alexie said from the next row, leaning over so far her chair squeaked. "Zero isn't prime. Ask literally anyone." Ryan felt his confidence evaporate, right there, like steam off the radiator by the window. He read his loop again. It started checking at 2. For 0, it checked 2, then 3, then stopped at nothing, found no dividers, and declared victory. The program wasn't broken; it was confidently wrong, which was somehow worse.

"So the numbers below 2 need their own rule," Ryan said slowly, mostly to himself. "Zero, one, and negative numbers aren't prime, but the loop never kicks them out because it starts at 2." Alexie tapped his screen. "Then make the program say not prime for anything less than 2 first, before the loop even starts."

He added two lines: if the number was less than 2, print "not prime," and skip the rest. He typed 0. "0 is not prime." He typed 1, then minus 5, then 13, and the answers came back correct every time, like a dog that had finally learned not to eat shoes. Grady peered over, red screen still glowing on his face, looking like a refugee from a technology disaster. "Is that a legitimate fix," he asked, "or did you just break it somewhere I can't see?"

Ryan slid his chair over. "Type something," he said. "Try to break it."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: The Sieve of Eratosthenes, an ancient Greek method, lists primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn.
story:
Jayden sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with the old laptop open in front of him. His program was due Monday, and so far all it did was crash. He was supposed to write a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime, but every time he typed 9, the screen said "prime" in bright letters, which was wrong, and he knew it was wrong, but he could not see why.

"You look like a man fighting an invisible enemy," his grandfather said, setting down two glasses of milk.

"It's my code. It says 9 is prime. Something's wrong in there, but I can't see inside it." Jayden stared at the lines on the screen. The program was just text, quiet and unreadable, hiding its mistake somewhere between the input and the answer.

His grandfather disappeared into the hall closet and came back with a brittle old paperback, its spine cracked and its pages yellow. He flipped it open to a folded page and smoothed it flat. There was a grid of numbers, 2 through 100, with circles and lines through them in faded pencil. "I made this when I was about your age," he said. "My teacher called it the Sieve of Eratosthenes. An ancient Greek method. You list the primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn." He tapped the grid. "Do it yourself and you'll see which answers your machine is getting wrong."

Jayden pulled a blank sheet of paper and copied the numbers 1 to 50 in rows. He started with 2 and crossed out every second number after it, then 3 and every third number, then 5, then 7. When he reached 9, it was already crossed out, because 3 had taken it. That was it. His program was checking whether a number divided evenly by anything only after some wrong spot in the loop, so it never actually tested the case that mattered. He found the line, fixed the greater-than sign, and ran it again. He typed 9 and the screen printed "not prime." He typed 91, and the program said "not prime," which matched his grid, since 7 had crossed it out. He typed 53 and got "prime," and on his paper 53 sat there untouched, circled and whole.

He kept going, testing every number on the grid, his pencil checking against the machine like a laser line, back and forth. His grandfather watched over his shoulder, saying nothing. Somewhere down the block a dog began to bark, and the afternoon light moved slowly across the table. Jayden reached the last number, 97, still uncrossed, and typed it in.

"Prime," said the screen, and Jayden, without looking up, whispered, "Prime," along with it.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Specific details, like 'Grandma's red bicycle' instead of 'a bike', give an improv partner more to build on.
story:
Alexis stood in the wings of the dilapidated community theatre, where the paint on the walls was peeling like old sunburn, and watched Ms. Sutherland write one word on the whiteboard: YES. The improv workshop had ten kids in it, and Alexis had only come because Alix had begged her, promising it would be better than sitting at home all summer.

"Two people, one scene," Ms. Sutherland said. "Whatever your partner offers, you accept it and add to it. Yes, and."

Bastien went first with Alix, and their scene worked. Then it was Alexis's turn. Bastien walked onstage, mimed setting down a heavy box, and said, "Okay, I brought the stuff."

"Great," Alexis said, her mind blank. "We have... the stuff."

"Yeah," Bastien said. "The stuff."

They stared at each other. Alexis offered, "It's heavy," and Bastien said, "Yep," and after thirty more seconds of nothing Ms. Sutherland called time. Alexis's face burned. She had assumed the problem was that she was bad at improv, but sitting backstage afterward, watching the next pair, she started to wonder if the problem was something else. The pair onstage was talking about borrowing "Grandma's red bicycle," and suddenly they had a whole argument going, complete with a bent fender and a missing bell. It wasn't talent. It was that the red bicycle gave them something to grab onto, and "the stuff" had given Bastien and her nothing.

She found Bastien by the water fountain. "Can we try again? I have an idea."

"Sure," he said, though he looked doubtful.

Back onstage, Bastien set down his invisible box the same way. "Okay, I brought the stuff."

"Yes," Alexis said, "and it's your grandfather's antique telescope, the one you weren't supposed to touch."

Bastien's whole posture changed. He lifted the box as if it held glass. "And the lens is cracked," he said. "You were supposed to be watching it."

"I was watching," Alexis said, "but a raccoon knocked it over."

"There's no raccoons on the roof."

"There are now. Three of them." The scene ran for five whole minutes, through the raccoon chase and a call to an imaginary animal control officer who turned out to be Bastien's uncle, until Ms. Sutherland laughed and clapped from the third row.

Afterward Alix jogged over. "That was so much better. What happened?"

"I changed my mind about what the problem was," Alexis said. She was still a little amazed by it. "It was never that I couldn't think of anything. It's that 'the stuff' gave us nothing to build on, and a cracked telescope with a raccoon problem gives you everything."

"Grandma's red bicycle," Alix said, grinning. "That's what did it for me."

Ms. Sutherland wrote a new word under YES on the whiteboard: SPECIFIC. Then she turned and said, "Alexis and Bastien, show them again, from the top."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice.
story:
Elijah sat at the old upright piano on the school auditorium stage, glaring at the page. The same eight measures had defeated him all through Thursday's practice, and his fingers still tripped in exactly the same place. "Again," said Mr. Foster from the third row of seats, and Elijah played it, and the third note of the left hand landed late again, like always.

"It's not fair," Elijah said. "I can play every other part. This part isn't even hard. It looks trivial on the page." Mr. Foster stood up and walked toward the stage. "Then your eyes are playing tricks on you. Easy on the page and easy in the hands are two different things. It's an illusion that the notes being simple means the passage is simple." He tapped the measure with one finger. "Play it ten more times tonight, slow, and let it go. The concert is Saturday."

Brian and Darien came in through the side door carrying folding chairs for the chorus risers. "Still stuck on that part?" Brian called. "Since Tuesday," Elijah said. Darien set down his stack of chairs. "My cousin had the same thing with a drum solo. She practiced until she was furious, went to bed mad, and the next morning she could just play it. She didn't touch the drums in between, either. She swears the sleep did the practicing for her."

Elijah didn't believe it, exactly, but that night he ran the eight measures ten slow times, packed up, and went to bed. He did not sneak back to the piano for extra work, even though he wanted to. He lay in the dark worrying that he had wasted the whole evening.

Friday morning before school, the auditorium was unlocked, so he climbed onto the stage and opened the music. He set his hands on the keys, half expecting to perceive nothing new, just the same clumsy passage in the same stubborn fingers. He played it. It worked. He played it again, faster, and it worked again, the left hand landing exactly where it belonged. No extra practice had happened, none at all, and yet the passage had somehow fixed itself overnight, and the surprise of it made him laugh out loud in the empty hall.

At rehearsal, Brian and Darien were hauling chairs again. "Guess what," Elijah said, and played the whole piece start to finish, including the eight measures, without a single stumble. Mr. Foster raised his eyebrows. "Well," he said. "What happened between yesterday and today?" Elijah grinned and looked at Darien. "Your cousin was right. A night of sleep after practicing did it, and I didn't practice one bit more." Mr. Foster shook his head slowly and said, "Play it once more, from the top."
